record.paper_title: Measurement of Energy Spectrum and Elemental Composition of PeV Cosmic Rays: Open Problems and Prospects
record.original_question: What unknown systematic uncertainties make direct, indirect, and ground-array measurements of the 100 TeV–100 PeV cosmic-ray spectrum and composition conflict, and how can experiment designs disentangle the effects of altitude, detector coverage, muon measurements, shower-core observables, reconstruction procedures, and hadronic-interaction models?

evidence.quote: In fact, important results obtained by ‘direct’ methods are conflicting due to some still unknown systematic uncertainties probably related to the interaction model used to assign the energy.

These results cannot be reconciled and show the existence of a still unknown systematic uncertainty that, as discussed in previous sections, could be due to the different array characteristics (altitude, coverage), the observables used (muons or shower core characteristics), and the dependence on hadronic interaction models.

The experimental situation in the 100 TeV–100 PeV energy region must be clarified to solve the longstanding problem of the origin of the knee and to give solid foundations to CR models up to the highest observed energies. A new experiment, able to measure, at the right altitude and with high statistics, the elemental composition exploiting the techniques used so far in different apparatus, is mandatory to investigate the unknown uncertainties affecting the results so far obtained by shower arrays.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider measurements of the all-particle cosmic-ray energy spectrum and elemental (mass) composition in the energy range 100 TeV to 100 PeV, which spans the so-called "knee" region. Three complementary classes of experiments contribute data:

(a) Direct measurements performed by balloon- or satellite-borne detectors above the atmosphere, which identify primary nuclei directly but have limited exposure;
(b) Indirect ground-based measurements that observe extensive air showers via Cherenkov light, fluorescence, or radio emission;
(c) Ground arrays of surface (and possibly underground) particle detectors, which sample the secondary particle densities of extensive air showers at one or more altitudes, and may include separate muon detectors and/or shower-core ("core observables") sub-arrays.

Reconstruction of primary energy E and primary mass A from indirect data depends on: the observation altitude (atmospheric depth at detection), the detector area and lateral coverage, the choice of observables (e.g., electromagnetic size N_e, muon size N_μ, shower-core particle density, depth of shower maximum X_max), the reconstruction algorithms, and the hadronic-interaction model used in Monte Carlo simulations (e.g., QGSJET-II, EPOS-LHC, SIBYLL).

Currently the published spectra and mass compositions from different experiments in this energy range disagree by amounts exceeding their quoted statistical and known systematic uncertainties, indicating one or more unidentified systematic effects.

Problem. Identify and quantify the unknown systematic uncertainties responsible for the disagreement among direct, indirect, and ground-array measurements of the primary cosmic-ray energy spectrum and elemental composition in the 100 TeV–100 PeV range. Specifically, design an experimental program (including choice of altitude, detector coverage, muon detection capability, shower-core observables, reconstruction procedure, and treatment of hadronic-interaction-model dependence) that can simultaneously and self-consistently disentangle the contributions of each of these factors to the observed discrepancies, and thereby produce a reconciled measurement of the spectrum and composition across the knee region.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is a programmatic experimental open problem in cosmic-ray physics. As of recent literature, the discrepancies among direct, indirect, and ground-array measurements in the knee region remain unresolved, with hadronic-interaction-model uncertainties (notably the long-standing muon excess / "muon puzzle") still under active investigation. No experiment has yet definitively disentangled all listed systematics.

status_evidence.title: The Muon Puzzle in cosmic-ray induced air showers
status_evidence.snippet: Reviews the persistent discrepancy between measured and simulated muon numbers in extensive air showers and its impact on mass composition measurements.
status_evidence.claim: Hadronic-interaction-model systematics in air-shower observables remain an unresolved problem.

status_evidence.title: Measurement of Energy Spectrum and Elemental Composition of PeV Cosmic Rays: Open Problems and Prospects
status_evidence.snippet: Review identifies unknown systematic uncertainties causing conflicts among measurements in 100 TeV–100 PeV range and calls for a new experiment.
status_evidence.claim: The problem is explicitly framed as open and requiring a new dedicated experiment.
